q: "Reduce aged reconciliation breaks by 40% within 12 months" is an example of which requirement type?
why: Business requirements state organizational goals and objectives, the 'why'.

q: "The system shall automatically match transactions with the same amount, value date and reference." What type is this?
why: It describes a behavior the system must perform, which makes it functional.

q: "The matching run shall finish within 15 minutes for 200,000 transactions." What type is this?
why: It defines how well the system performs, a quality attribute, so it is non-functional.

q: Which is a transition requirement?
options: Migrate open breaks from the old system with their original age
Log every manual match for audit
why: Transition requirements are temporary capabilities needed to move from the current to the future state, such as data migration and training.

q: "Only users with the Reconciler role can approve write-offs" is best classified as a…
why: Access control is a security quality attribute (some teams also record it as a business rule).

q: "Breaks older than 30 days must be escalated to the team lead" is best described as a…
why: A business rule is a policy or constraint that guides behavior, independent of the system that enforces it.

q: Which document's main purpose is to justify an investment with options, costs, benefits and a recommendation?
why: A business case justifies whether the initiative is worth doing.

q: A BRD is primarily written for…
why: The Business Requirements Document captures what the business needs, for business stakeholders.

q: In a use case, the 'alternate flow' describes…
options: A valid variation from the main success path
why: Alternate flows are valid variations, such as a team lead rejecting rather than approving a match.

q: "We believe the bank's statement feed will remain in MT940 format." This is a…
why: An assumption is believed true but not confirmed, and it should be tracked as a risk.

q: "The solution must go live before financial year end." This is a…
why: A constraint is a limit the project must work within.

q: Why should a BRD include an explicit 'out of scope' list?
options: To prevent misunderstandings and arguments about what will be delivered
Because templates require it but it has no value
why: Clear out-of-scope statements manage expectations and reduce scope creep.

q: Which is the standard user story format?
options: As a <user>, I want <goal>, so that <benefit>
why: User stories use 'As a… I want… so that…'. Given/When/Then is for acceptance criteria.

q: Why is the 'so that' clause important in a user story?
options: It records the value, letting the team find the best solution
why: 'So that' captures the reason and benefit, keeping the focus on value rather than a fixed solution.

q: In INVEST, what does the 'S' stand for?
why: INVEST: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable.

q: A story can't be estimated because the team doesn't understand it. Which INVEST criterion fails?
why: Estimable means the team understands the story well enough to size it.

q: What are the 'three Cs' of a user story?
why: Card (the written statement), Conversation (the details discussed) and Confirmation (the acceptance criteria).

q: A large body of work too big for one sprint, such as 'Automated APAC reconciliation', is called…
why: Epics are large items that are broken down into features and stories.

q: What is the recommended way to split a large user story?
options: Vertically, so each slice delivers usable end-to-end value
Horizontally by layer: database first, then UI
why: Vertical slices deliver working value each sprint; horizontal slices don't deliver value until all layers are done.

q: In Gherkin, what does the 'Given' step describe?
why: Given sets the context, When is the action and Then is the expected outcome.

q: Which acceptance criterion is best written?
options: An item with a value date 31 days ago is shown with a red indicator
why: It is specific and testable. The others are vague.

q: The rule is 'highlight items older than 30 days'. Which scenario tests the boundary?
options: An item exactly 30 days old is not highlighted
An item 300 days old is highlighted
why: Boundary tests check values at the edge of a rule, where defects are most common.

q: When should acceptance criteria be agreed?
options: Only when a defect is found
why: Agreeing criteria early aligns developers, testers and the PO and prevents rework.

q: How does the Definition of Done differ from acceptance criteria?
options: DoD applies to every story; acceptance criteria are specific to one story
Acceptance criteria apply to the whole project
DoD is written by the customer only
why: The DoD is a shared quality checklist for all work items; acceptance criteria define one story's specific conditions.

q: What is wrong with 'The system shall export to Excel and email the report'?
options: It is not atomic; it combines two requirements
why: Atomic requirements contain one need each, so they can be tested and traced separately.

q: Which word makes a requirement ambiguous?
why: Words like 'fast', 'easy' and 'user-friendly' have no single measurable meaning.

q: A tester says they can't work out how to test a requirement. Which quality characteristic is missing?
why: If the requirement can't be tested, it can't be proven met. Make it specific and measurable.

q: Linking a requirement back to the business objective it supports is called…
why: Backward traceability connects requirements to their source or objective.

q: A stakeholder changes a requirement. What does the RTM help you do first?
options: Analyze the impact on designs and test cases
why: Traceability shows every artifact linked to the requirement, which makes impact analysis fast.

q: Before go-live, the test manager asks whether every requirement has been tested. Which artifact answers this?
why: Forward traceability in the RTM links each requirement to its test cases and status.

q: In MoSCoW, a regulatory requirement without which the release cannot go live is a…
why: Must haves are critical, often legal or core functions.

q: In MoSCoW, what does 'W' mean?
why: 'Won't have (this time)' is an explicit agreement to exclude an item from this release.

q: In the Kano model, a feature customers expect and are dissatisfied without is a…
why: Basic features are expected; having them doesn't delight, but lacking them causes dissatisfaction.

q: WSJF prioritizes work by…
options: Cost of delay divided by job size
why: Weighted Shortest Job First (SAFe) favors items with high cost of delay and small size.

q: What is a requirements baseline?
options: An approved version of requirements after which changes are formally controlled
The first draft of the requirements
why: A baseline is an approved snapshot; changes after it go through change control.

q: A senior manager asks for a new feature two weeks before go-live. What should the BA do?
options: Log it, analyze impact, and present options to the decision maker
Add it immediately to keep the manager happy
Tell the developers to build it quietly
why: Change control means assessing impact on scope, schedule, cost and risk, then letting the authorized person decide.

q: Uncontrolled growth in project scope is called…
why: Scope creep is uncontrolled expansion. (Gold plating is adding features nobody asked for.)
